n: The prayer from chapter 63 continues with a passionate cry: “Oh, that You would tear open the heavens and come down,” so that mountains would melt before You. D&C 133 quotes this in describing the Second Coming.

f.w: Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens

n: Come like a fire that sets brushwood ablaze and makes water boil, so Your enemies know Your name and the nations tremble.

f.w: the nations may tremble at thy presence

n: Remember when You did awesome things we never expected, came down, and the mountains shook—as at Mount Sinai.

f.w: the mountains flowed down at thy presence

n: Since the world began no one has heard or seen any God besides You who acts for those who wait for Him. Paul adapts this to say no eye has seen what God has prepared for those who love Him; the Lord echoes it in D&C 76.
God meets those who gladly do right and remember His ways. But we sinned and He was angry. The last line is hard to translate; the KJV hopes that by continuing in God’s ways “we shall be saved.”

f.w: Thou meetest him that rejoiceth and worketh righteousness

f.g: In Your ways is permanence; the Hebrew here is difficult.

n: A famous confession: we have all become unclean, and even our best deeds are like stained rags. We wither like leaves, and our sins blow us away like wind. Without God’s grace, human goodness can’t save us.

f.w: all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags
we all do fade as a leaf

n: No one calls on God’s name or stirs himself to hold on to Him, because God has hidden His face and let them melt away in their sins.

f.w: stirreth up himself to take hold of thee

n: “But now, Lord, You are our Father. We are the clay; You are the potter. We are all the work of Your hands.” An appeal to God’s love as Creator and Father, and a humble willingness to be reshaped.

f.w: we are the clay, and thou our potter

n: Please don’t be angry beyond measure or remember our sins forever. Look—we are all Your people.
Your holy cities have become a desert; Zion is a wilderness and Jerusalem a ruin.
Our holy and beautiful temple, where our ancestors praised You, has been burned, and all our treasures lie in ruins. The Babylonians burned Solomon’s temple in 586 BC.
After all this, will You hold back, Lord? Will You stay silent and keep afflicting us so severely? The prayer ends with an open question that chapter 65 answers.
